docs.title: Apps hosted on the platform
docs.text:
# Secret Where Read by Rotation today Target Owner Risk 29 Database passwords: Keycloak, n8n, roadmap, qcm, sessions keycloak/db, n8n/db, roadmap/config, qcm/config, 3istor-sessions/config The apps Never Vault database secrets engine or the CNPG-generated secret infra, app teams Medium 30 App keys: n8n encryption key, Flask secret (MEPA), NextAuth (qcm), sessions app secret, roadmap webhook and cron secrets n8n/encryption-key, mepa-app/config, qcm/config, 3istor-sessions/config, roadmap/config The apps Never Stay static by nature app teams Low 31 MEPA Gemini API key mepa-app/config MEPA Never Vertex AI with GCP Workload Identity Federation (already used by the CMP for billing) MEPA team Medium 32 linmap-bot: Google service account JSON key, Linear API key, Discord bot token linmap-bot/config linmap-bot Never Google: Workload Identity Federation instead of the JSON key. Linear and Discord stay static linmap team Medium 33 Notion API key (roadmap), Google OAuth client secret (sessions) roadmap/config, 3istor-sessions/config roadmap, sessions Never Stay static app teams Medium 34 Project secrets entered in the CMP, project tunnel tokens kvv2/projects/*, project-<name>/* mounts Project apps By the project Per project project teams Varies

34 entries. The five riskiest, in order:

  1. Keycloak master admin (#1): owns every realm, so every login of the platform and of the projects. Three copies, one of them in a running pod.
  2. GitHub App private key (#3): write access to the repositories Argo CD deploys from, so code in the cluster; it can also push to main of cnp-projects, which keeps a ruleset bypass for the CMP.
  3. OpenStack password (#13): the project that hosts the cluster's nodes, handed to a CI outside the platform repositories as well.
  4. Ceph keys, RGW admin-ops first (#17, #18): every bucket and volume, backups and logs included.
  5. Cloudflare API token (#5): DNS of the zone, so certificates and traffic of every public route.

The CMP Vault token (#2) would top the list; it is left out because its replacement is already deployed and only the removal remains.

docs.title: Findings to fix
docs.text:
• App icon keys are outside Terraform. icons-s3-access-key-id and icons-s3-secret-access-key are read by the CMP from arcl-cmp/credentials, but the vault_kv_secret_v2.arcl_cmp_creds resource does not declare them. The next terraform apply of K3s/terraform writes a version without them and the CMP loses its icon bucket. Add them as variables before the next apply.
  • One OIDC client secret in ten places (#8). A leak from any app opens Grafana, the CMP and every protected app route.
  • Unused S3 keys in observability/config (#28).
  • dockair CI gets the platform's OpenStack and AWS credentials (#13, #14) through Vault. The login is federated, the credentials behind it are not.

docs.title: Measuring their age
docs.text:
Vault KV v2 keeps the created_time of every version of a path. The secret-age CronJob (K3s/k8s/config/observability/secret-age.yaml) reads it every hour and pushes cnp_secret_age_days{path} to VictoriaMetrics: the days since the current version of each kvv2 path was written.

  • It logs in with its own service account (Vault role secret-age) whose policy only allows list and read on kvv2/metadata/*. It never reads a value.
  • Alert StaticSecretOlderThan90Days (vmalert, static-secrets.rules) fires for any platform path older than 90 days. Project paths (kvv2/projects/*) are measured but not alerted on: their owners rotate them.
  • Alert SecretAgeExporterFailed fires when a run fails, like AuditArchiveFailed for the audit archive.
# Oldest platform secrets first
sort_desc(max by (path) (max_over_time(cnp_secret_age_days{path!~"kvv2/projects/.*"}[2h])))

Limits:

  • The age is per path, not per key. A path holding many keys (arcl-cmp/credentials holds 35) gets younger as soon as one key is written, even if the others stay. Splitting such paths by credential makes the metric honest.
  • Not measured: the Rook-generated S3 keys (#19, Kubernetes Secrets), the project-* mounts (#34), the Vault auth configs (#16), the unseal keys (#12) and the Cloud Terraform variables (#21 to #23). They are outside kvv2.

docs.title: Conformité CIS : preuves hebdomadaires
docs.text: Chaque semaine, la plateforme on-prem est comparée au CIS Kubernetes Benchmark, au guide NSA-CISA et à MITRE ATT&CK. Les rapports sont rangés dans l'archive d'audit verrouillée (voir Journaux d'audit) : ce sont les preuves de l'item A1. Le code est dans K3s/k8s/config/compliance/.

docs.title: Ce qui tourne
docs.text:
CronJob (compliance) Outil Ce qui est vérifié Quand (UTC) kube-bench-server kube-bench v0.16.0, profil k3s-cis-1.9 serveur my-k3s-cluster-node : cibles master, controlplane, node, policies dimanche 03:00 kube-bench-agent kube-bench v0.16.0, profil k3s-cis-1.9 agent k3s-worker-node : cible node dimanche 03:00 kubescape Kubescape v4.0.20, regolibrary v2.0.39 objets de l'API : cis-v1.12.0, nsa, mitre dimanche 03:30

Les images sont épinglées par digest. Un job en échec déclenche l'alerte vmalert ComplianceScanFailed.

Un job kube-bench par rôle de nœud, placé par nodeSelector (serveur) ou affinité (tout nœud sans rôle control-plane) : le cluster a un serveur et un agent. Avec un deuxième agent, il faudra une copie de kube-bench-agent par nœud, épinglée par kubernetes.io/hostname.

docs.title: Où sont les résultats
docs.text:
Bucket RGW cnp-audit-archive, préfixe compliance/ :

compliance/kube-bench/AAAA-MM-JJ/<nœud>.json      rapport complet (--json, sorties des tests incluses)
compliance/kubescape/AAAA-MM-JJ/onprem.json       rapport complet (format json)
compliance/summary/AAAA-MM-JJ/<outil>-<cible>.json  compteurs pour le portail

Le résumé donne pass, fail, warn (et info pour kube-bench) avec la version de l'outil et le chemin du rapport. Pour Kubescape, les compteurs portent sur les contrôles et warn compte les contrôles skipped (revue manuelle, ou type de ressource non lu), avec le score de conformité par framework.

Les objets suivent les règles du bucket : Object Lock COMPLIANCE 180 jours, expiration à 190 jours. L'utilisateur RGW compliance-scans ne peut qu'écrire sous compliance/ (bucket policy posée par le job audit-archive) : il ne lit ni ne supprime rien. Pour lire un rapport, utiliser l'utilisateur audit-archive :

aws --endpoint-url http://192.168.1.110:7480 s3 ls s3://cnp-audit-archive/compliance/summary/ --recursive

Point zéro, scan Kubescape manuel du 13/11/2026 avec la même configuration : score 51,5 % (CIS 48,4 %, NSA 61,2 %, MITRE 58,0 %).

docs.title: Pourquoi un namespace privilégié
docs.text:
Les contrôles CIS des nœuds lisent les drapeaux des processus k3s, les droits des fichiers sous /var/lib/rancher et /etc/rancher, et le journal systemd de l'unité k3s. Le pod kube-bench a donc hostPID, des montages hostPath en lecture seule (dont / sur /host), tourne en root et garde deux capacités : SYS_CHROOT (lancer le journalctl du nœud, absent de l'image) et DAC_READ_SEARCH. Aucun niveau Pod Security sous privileged ne le permet.

Ce qui l'isole :

  • le namespace compliance ne contient que ces trois CronJobs, sans Service, entrées réseau refusées par NetworkPolicy ;
  • le conteneur d'envoi, non root et sans capacité, est le seul à voir le secret RGW ;
  • le pod Kubescape respecte le niveau restricted (vérifié en dry-run), le label pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted signale tout écart ;
  • les ClusterRoles sont en lecture seule (get, list). Celui de Kubescape ne lit pas les Secrets ; celui de kube-bench ne lit que pods, service accounts et objets RBAC.

docs.title: Contrôles que K3s traite autrement
docs.text:
D'après les notes de remédiation du profil k3s-cis-1.9 et la configuration du serveur :

Contrôles Pourquoi 1.1.1 à 1.1.8 API server, controller manager, scheduler et etcd tournent dans le processus k3s : pas de manifeste de pod statique. kube-bench les marque skip. 1.1.11, 1.1.12, section 2 (etcd) Le serveur unique stocke son état dans SQLite (kine), pas dans etcd. La cible etcd n'est pas lancée. À revoir si le cluster passe en etcd embarqué. 4.1.1, 4.1.2, 4.1.9, 4.1.10 Le kubelet est embarqué : pas de fichier de service ni de fichier de configuration. 4.2.7 K3s pose --hostname-override, ce que le CIS admet. 4.1.3, 4.1.4, 4.3.1 et Kubescape C-0291 kube-proxy est désactivé (--disable-kube-proxy), Cilium le remplace. 1.1.9, 1.1.10 Les fichiers CNI sont ceux de Cilium ; un fichier de verrou en 750 est attendu.

docs.title: Choix de la plateforme
docs.text: Contrôles Pourquoi 1.2.17, 1.2.18 (audit-log-maxage, audit-log-maxbackup) Le fichier d'audit local n'est qu'un tampon (2 jours, 3 fichiers) : Alloy l'envoie dans Loki (30 jours) puis dans l'archive verrouillée (180 jours). 1.2.11 (AlwaysPullImages) Le profil K3s le classe « permissif » : chaque démarrage de pod dépendrait du registre. Version du profil kube-bench v0.16.0 n'a pas de profil K3s plus récent que k3s-cis-1.9 (CIS 1.9, Kubernetes 1.27) ; le cluster est en 1.34. Les objets de l'API sont couverts en CIS 1.12 par Kubescape. Kubescape C-0212 (CIS 5.6.4) Le scanner ne lit pas les Secrets : la partie « Secrets dans default » n'est pas évaluée. Contrôles d'hôte Kubescape --host-scan=false : ils déploieraient un capteur privilégié ; kube-bench couvre les nœuds.

docs.title: Écarts réels, à corriger
docs.text:
Les drapeaux du serveur (journal k3s du 12/11/2026) annoncent ces FAIL. Ce ne sont pas des écarts acceptés :

  • 1.2.27, 1.2.28 : pas de chiffrement des Secrets au repos (--secrets-encryption) ;
  • 1.2.9 : pas de plugin d'admission EventRateLimit ;
  • 1.2.3 : DenyServiceExternalIPs n'est pas activé.

docs.title: Lancer un passage à la main
docs.text:
kubectl -n compliance create job kube-bench-server-manual --from=cronjob/kube-bench-server
kubectl -n compliance create job kube-bench-agent-manual --from=cronjob/kube-bench-agent
kubectl -n compliance create job kubescape-manual --from=cronjob/kubescape
kubectl -n compliance logs job/kubescape-manual -c upload

Le conteneur upload affiche le résumé. Relancer le même jour crée une nouvelle version des objets ; l'ancienne reste verrouillée.

docs.title: Limites
docs.text:
• Kubescape télécharge la regolibrary épinglée depuis GitHub à chaque passage : sans accès sortant, le job échoue.
  • Les contrôles qui lisent le journal (drapeaux des composants) dépendent de la ligne « Running kube-apiserver » écrite au démarrage de k3s. Le journal est persistant sur les nœuds, mais une rotation après un long uptime peut faire passer ces contrôles en WARN.
  • Comme pour l'archive d'audit, un admin Ceph peut effacer le bucket avec radosgw-admin.

docs.title: CMP Portal Architecture & Dashboard
docs.text: The Cloud Management Platform (CMP) is the developer-facing Internal Developer Portal (IDP). It is designed as a Multi-Provider Hybrid Portal, allowing developers to deploy and manage legacy IaaS stacks (AWS Auto Scaling Groups + OpenStack DB) alongside modern K3s GitOps workloads from a single interface.

docs.title: 1. Directory & Codebase Layout
docs.text:
The CMP codebase is structured as a monorepo to maintain strong contract alignments between the Next.js frontend schemas and the FastAPI routers.

arcl-cmp/
├── backend/
│   ├── app/
│   │   ├── core/              # Config, DB connections, and WAL initialization
│   │   ├── models/            # SQLAlchemy database entities (Deployments, Project Owners)
│   │   ├── schemas/           # Pydantic payloads and validation models
│   │   ├── routers/           # FastAPI HTTP endpoints (deployments, projects, catalog, account)
│   │   ├── services/          # Pure domain logic (SAGA, Keycloak admin, GitHub App, Vault VSO)
│   │   └── terraform/         # Day-0 Bootstrapping local modules (github_bootstrap)
│   └── alembic/               # Database migrations
└── frontend/
    └── src/
        ├── app/               # Next.js App Router folders (account, projects, auth)
        ├── components/        
        │   ├── account/       # GitHubLinkButton (OAuth installation callback)
        │   ├── catalog/       # CatalogGrid, DeployModal
        │   ├── dashboard/     # Overall health summaries
        │   └── projects/      # AppCard, AppConfigPanel (GitOps), MembersPanel
        ├── lib/               # API clients, custom React hooks
        └── types/             # Shared TypeScript interface definitions

docs.title: 2. Backend Orchestration (The SAGA Strategy)
docs.text: The saga_orchestrator.py service acts as the central workflow router. It executes different state-machine paths depending on the template's provider_type.

docs.title: A. The SAGA Execution Flow:
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Start([POST /api/deployments]) --> Validate[Validate Pydantic Schema]
    Validate --> Route{Check provider_type}

    %% Kubernetes Path
    Route -->|KUBERNETES| PathK8s[Kubernetes GitOps Flow]
    PathK8s --> K8s_Token[1. Mint GitHub App Token]
    K8s_Token --> K8s_TF[2. Execute github_bootstrap module]
    K8s_TF -->|Writes-back values.yaml, applies App CRD| K8s_DB[3. Save State S3 path & outputs to DB]
    K8s_DB --> K8s_Argo[4. Handover to ArgoCD]
    K8s_Argo --> K8s_Success([Status: RUNNING])

    %% Legacy Path
    Route -->|LEGACY_HYBRID| PathLegacy[Legacy Hybrid Flow]
    PathLegacy --> Leg_OS[1. Provision OpenStack DB VMs]
    Leg_OS -->|Success| Leg_AWS[2. Provision AWS ASG & ALB]
    Leg_AWS -->|Success| Leg_Success([Status: RUNNING])

    %% Legacy Rollback
    Leg_AWS -->|Failure| Leg_Rollback[SAGA Rollback: Terminate OpenStack VMs]
    Leg_Rollback --> Leg_Fail([Status: FAILED])
    Leg_OS -->|Failure| Leg_Fail

docs.title: 3. Multi-Provider Health Monitoring (Strategy Pattern)
docs.text:
The monitoring_service.py is implemented using a Strategy Pattern. When the frontend or the background poller queries the health status of a deployment, the service routes the request to the correct cloud provider SDK:

flowchart LR
    CMP[GET /api/deployments/id] --> Check{Check provider_type}

    %% Legacy Routing
    Check -->|LEGACY_HYBRID| MonitorLegacy[Legacy Strategy]
    MonitorLegacy -->|Boto3 API| AWS_ALB[Query AWS ALB Target Group]
    MonitorLegacy -->|OpenStack SDK| OS_VMs[Query OpenStack compute.servers]
    AWS_ALB & OS_VMs --> MergeLegacy[Consolidate States]

    %% Kubernetes Routing
    Check -->|KUBERNETES| MonitorK8s[Kubernetes Strategy]
    MonitorK8s -->|ArgoCD REST API| Argo_Server[Query /api/v1/applications/name]
    Argo_Server --> MergeK8s[Map ArgoCD Status to CMP Status]

    MergeLegacy & MergeK8s --> Return[Return AppHealthResponse]

docs.title: ArgoCD to CMP Status Mapping:
docs.text: When querying a Kubernetes-native GitOps deployment, the backend translates ArgoCD's statuses into standardized CMP states: * ArgoCD Healthy & Synced ➔ CMP healthy * ArgoCD Progressing ➔ CMP deploying * ArgoCD Degraded or OutOfSync ➔ CMP degraded * ArgoCD Missing or Unknown ➔ CMP failed

docs.title: 4. Frontend Dynamic Components
docs.text: The Next.js frontend uses conditional rendering to adapt components to the underlying infrastructure type.

docs.title: A. The Dynamic DeploymentCard.tsx
docs.text:
• For Legacy Deployments: Displays the public AWS Application Load Balancer DNS endpoint and raw OpenStack VM IP addresses.
  • For Kubernetes Deployments: Renders deep-link action buttons pointing directly to the Git repository, the matching ArgoCD Application dashboard, and the project's HashiCorp Vault namespace.

docs.title: B. The AppConfigPanel.tsx (Day-2 GitOps Editor)
docs.text:
When viewing a kubernetes deployment, the frontend renders a dedicated configuration editor. It fetches the live, commented values.yaml from GitHub, renders inputs (sliders for replicas, switches for SSO), and executes deep-merge PATCH commits on save, bypassing the Kubernetes API.

Next Step: Continue to Keycloak Identity & Access Management.

docs.title: Identity & Access Management: Keycloak Integration
docs.text: Keycloak serves as the central Identity Provider (IdP) for the entire CNP ecosystem. It secures the developer portal (CMP), infrastructure platforms (Vault, ArgoCD), and deployed end-user applications via Envoy Gateway edge routing. The central instance runs Keycloak 26.8.1 (see section 6).

docs.title: 1. Custom Theme Extraction Pipeline (DevOps)
docs.text:
To provide a cohesive brand identity for the portal, CNP implements a customized theme named keycloak-theme-kube-lab.

Instead of baking the theme directly into a heavy, custom Keycloak container image, CNP uses a decoupled, declarative InitContainer Pipeline with shared Kubernetes volumes (emptyDir).

docs.title: Theme Synchronization Architecture:
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Pod [Keycloak Pod]
        subgraph InitContainer [InitContainer: theme-provider-init]
            Image[ghcr.io/thegostsniperfr/keycloak-theme-kube-lab@sha256:c31626bb...]
            Image -->|Extracts theme files| MountInit[/providers/]
        end

        subgraph MainContainer [MainContainer: keycloakx]
            MountMain[/opt/keycloak/providers/] -->|Loads theme on boot| KC[Keycloak Server Process]
        end

        Volume[(emptyDir: theme-providers)] <-->|Shared Volume| MountInit
        Volume <-->|Shared Volume| MountMain
    end

docs.title: Declarative Implementation (k8s/config/keycloak/values.yaml):
docs.text:
# Shared volume configuration
extraVolumes: |
  - name: theme-providers
    emptyDir: {}

# Mount shared volume to the main Keycloak container
extraVolumeMounts: |
  - name: theme-providers
    mountPath: /opt/keycloak/providers

# InitContainer copy-paste mechanism
extraInitContainers: |
  - name: theme-provider-init
    # Pinned: the theme overrides internal login templates and must be retested on every Keycloak bump.
    image: ghcr.io/thegostsniperfr/keycloak-theme-kube-lab@sha256:c31626bb1de27aea9339e6d8fab99d0d4b395c6165ee52f10698083e522dd37a
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    volumeMounts:
      - name: theme-providers
        mountPath: /providers

On pod startup, the theme-provider-init container copies its theme files into /providers (the shared volume) and exits. The main Keycloak container then starts, mounts the same volume at /opt/keycloak/providers, reads the theme files, and compiles the visual layer.

The theme image used to follow :latest with imagePullPolicy: Always, so a theme release could break the login page at any pod restart. It is now pinned on a digest: moving it is a deliberate change, made together with a Keycloak bump and followed by a login test.

docs.title: 2. Browser Authentication Flow (Browser-3-istor-Login-v4)
docs.text:
CNP enforces a secure, two-stage authentication and authorization flow. Even if an attacker compromises a user's credentials and passes MFA, Keycloak blocks access at the IdP level if the user lacks the explicit authorization role.

flowchart TD
    Start([Access Platform]) --> Step1{Phase 1: Login}

    %% Phase 1
    Step1 -->|SSO Active?| Cookie[Cookie Authenticator]
    Cookie -->|No| Kerberos[Kerberos / Spnego AD]
    Kerberos -->|No| Forms[Username / Password Form]

    Forms --> MFA{MFA Configured?}
    MFA -->|Yes| OTP[Enter OTP Code]
    MFA -->|No| ForceOTP[Force OTP Setup Screen]

    %% Phase 2
    Cookie & Kerberos & OTP & ForceOTP --> Step2{Phase 2: RBAC Wrapper}
    Step2 -->|User possesses 'openid_client_access'?| Allow([Grant Access Token])
    Step2 -->|User lacks role| Deny[Deny Access Authenticator]
    Deny --> Block([HTTP 403 / Access Blocked])

docs.title: Phase 1: Login Wrapper (SSO or Credentials)
docs.text:
1. Cookie (auth-cookie): Attempts transparent single sign-on if a browser session is active.
  2. Kerberos (auth-spnego): Attempts Active Directory SSO handshake.
  3. Forms Fallback (auth-username-password-form): Prompts for credentials if SSO fails.
  4. Mandatory OTP (auth-otp-form): Forces users to register and input a TOTP token (using Google Authenticator or similar) upon first login via keycloak_required_action.totp.

docs.title: Phase 2: RBAC Deny Wrapper
docs.text:
Once authenticated, Keycloak evaluates the user's role mappings: * The Constraint: The user must possess the openid_client_access role. * The Action: If the condition negate = "true" (the user does NOT possess the role) is met, Keycloak triggers the deny-access-authenticator, blocking token generation.

# terraform/auth_flow.tf extract
resource "keycloak_authentication_execution_config" "condition_role_config" {
  realm_id     = keycloak_realm.kube_lab.id
  execution_id = keycloak_authentication_execution.condition_role.id
  alias        = "deny-if-not-3-istor-access"

  config = {
    condUserRole = "openid_client_access"
    negate       = "true" # Triggers downstream deny-access-authenticator if absent
  }
}

docs.title: 3. Project Scopes & Group Mappings
docs.text: Keycloak maps tenant permissions into OIDC tokens to enforce downstream security boundaries.

docs.title: Project Group Convention
docs.text:
When a project is created, the CMP dynamically provisions three groups in the platform realm (3istor): * project-<project_name>-admins * project-<project_name>-members * project-<project_name>-guests

Each project realm (see section 4) has its own flat groups, filled at every broker login from the platform groups above (the mapper re-evaluates the claim each time, so removing someone from the platform group removes them from the realm group at their next login): * project-admins and project-members: the project's developers. These are the names applications and ingress.allowedGroups see. * users: only in the prod realm <p>, created when customer access is first set to companies or open, never in <p>-staging. It is the realm's default group: Keycloak adds it to every new account (sign-ups, accounts an app creates, service-account users, developers at their first broker login), so it does not mean "customer". Apps rely on organization membership instead.

docs.title: OIDC Scope Mapping (groups scope)
docs.text:
To transmit these memberships securely to downstream consumers (ArgoCD, Envoy Gateway, Vault), Keycloak maps group memberships into the JWT token payload.

# terraform/scopes.tf extract
resource "keycloak_openid_client_scope" "groups" {
  realm_id               = keycloak_realm.kube_lab.id
  name                   = "groups"
  include_in_token_scope = true
}

resource "keycloak_openid_group_membership_protocol_mapper" "group_mapper" {
  realm_id        = keycloak_realm.kube_lab.id
  client_scope_id = keycloak_openid_client_scope.groups.id
  name            = "group-mapper"
  claim_name      = "groups"
  full_path       = false # Outputs flat "project-alpha-admins" instead of "/project-alpha-admins"
}

docs.title: Downstream Consumption Matrix:
docs.text:
• ArgoCD: Reads the groups claim. If it contains project-alpha-admins, it grants sync/override permissions inside the matching project-alpha ArgoCD AppProject.
  • Envoy Gateway: Reads the groups claim of the project realm token at the edge. If ingress.allowedGroups is set and the user tries to access api.alpha.3istor.com without project-members or project-admins, Envoy blocks the connection. Token forwarding is described in the generic chart.
  • Vault: Maps the groups claim to a Vault identity group alias, granting access to the kvv2/data/projects/alpha/* path.

docs.title: 4. Project Realms
docs.text:
Each project owns its Keycloak realms for the end users of its apps. Developers log in there through a broker ("Log in with 3istor Platform", identity provider 3istor-platform) that points at a client of the platform realm.

Realm Created Sign-up Admin login (Vault, mount project-<p>) App clients <p> (prod) with the project closed, unless customer access is open keycloak-tenant-admin cnp-<p>-<app> <p>-staging at the first staging activation of an app never open keycloak-tenant-admin-staging cnp-<p>-<app>-stg

The staging realm has the same content as the prod one (broker client broker-<p>-staging in 3istor, groups project-members / project-admins with their mappers, groups scope, a local admin), so developers log in to staging with their usual account. It is created by the Terraform module app-templates/templates/k3s-gitops-app/staging-realm (state cnp/projects/<p>/_staging-realm) and destroyed with the project. A project name ending in -staging is refused.

  • Wiring: when staging is turned on, the CMP writes ingress.realm and auth.realm in deploy/env/staging/*.yaml, so the staging route authenticates against the staging realm. An app that validates tokens must therefore read its issuer per environment (https://auth.3istor.com/realms/<p>-staging); a prod issuer rejects every staging token.
  • Test accounts on staging: create them in the staging realm, with the console (https://admin-auth.3istor.com/admin/<p>-staging/console/, credentials in Vault) or, with customer access set to companies or open, through the staging app's own client.
  • Existing staging apps created before the staging realm existed are moved with python -m app.scripts.move_staging_realm <deployment id> (CMP backend, platform admin, one-off per app). The staging OIDC client is recreated in the new realm.
  • Own Keycloak: an app whose config sets keycloak_realm_id keeps that realm in staging. No <p>-staging is created for it and the move script has nothing to move.

docs.title: 5. Customer Access
docs.text:
How the end customers of a project's apps get an account. One mode per project: registration is a realm setting, so all apps of a project share it. closed by default.

Mode Registration in <p> Organizations, organization scope, app rights Customers get in through closed closed left as they are accounts the project creates companies closed on their company's identity provider (adding a client company) or an organization invitation open open on self-registration ("Register"), plus the above
  • Setting: project settings, Access, "Customer access" (project admins and platform admins). API: PUT /api/projects/{name}/customer-access with {"mode": "closed"|"companies"|"open"}, refused (403) for AI assistants because opening a project to the public is a person's decision. The mode is spec.customerAccess in the project registry; a record from before the modes with selfRegistration: true reads as open.
  • companies and open:
    • Organizations are enabled in <p> and <p>-staging. New accounts land in the default group users (created if missing), never in project-members.
    • Each app client gets a service account holding manage-organizations and manage-users of its own realm (never manage-realm; Keycloak grants viewing users with manage-users), and the organization default scope: the access token carries "organization": ["<alias>"] without the app asking for the scope (checked on Keycloak 26.8.1). Prod clients cnp-<p>-<app> get this in <p> only, staging clients cnp-<p>-<app>-stg in <p>-staging only.
    • Only open opens registration, and only in <p>. Staging never opens it.
  • Order: open saves the mode, then opens Keycloak; a Keycloak failure answers 502 with the mode saved, and sending it again retries. Every other mode updates Keycloak first, then the registry, so a failure never leaves registration open.
  • Re-applied when an app is created and when staging is activated, so new clients get their rights. Re-applying the app Terraform keeps the default scopes and service account the CMP added. A Keycloak failure never fails the deployment.
  • closed only closes registration. Organizations, accounts, group and service accounts stay.
  • No e-mail yet: the project realms have no SMTP, so no address verification and no organization invitation e-mail (an invitation works with registration closed once SMTP exists: the link opens registration for that address only). Until then, companies come in through their identity provider, and the app or a platform admin adds other members.
  • How an app uses it: with its own client id and secret (already delivered by Vault), the app gets a client_credentials token from its realm and calls /admin/realms/<realm>/organizations to create an organization and add a member. The app-side recipe is in the template's using-cnp-services/reference/identity.md.

docs.title: Adding a client company
docs.text:
Platform admins, in the console of <p> (https://admin-auth.3istor.com/admin/<p>/console/), and in <p>-staging for tests. The project must be in companies or open mode.

  1. Identity provider: Identity providers, OpenID Connect v1.0 (or SAML v2.0). Alias <company>-sso (EPITA: epita). Give the company the redirect URI https://auth.3istor.com/realms/<p>/broker/<alias>/endpoint and enter the client id and secret it returns. Trust email: on: Keycloak 26.8 adds a brokered account to an organization only if its address is verified.
  2. Organization: Organizations, Create. Name, alias (the company id apps store, fixed for good), and the company's e-mail domains. A domain belongs to one organization only.
  3. Link: the organization's Identity providers tab, link the provider, auto-membership on. A linked provider no longer shows as a button on the login page: people type their e-mail and step 4 sends them to their company, so the page stays the same whatever the number of companies. Unlinked providers (3istor Platform) keep their button.
  4. Routing: Domains tab, edit each domain: Identity provider = the alias above, Auto redirect on. Someone who types an address of that domain goes straight to the company's login. An account that already has a password is not redirected, so demo accounts keep logging in with theirs.
  5. Company administrators: the group the app expects (optispace: top-level group facility-managers, created once per realm). Add the administrator once their account exists, after their first login through the company.
  6. Check: log in to the app with an address of the company. The access token carries "organization": ["<alias>"].

Rules: an account belongs to one organization only, and apps refuse an account with several (optispace answers 403 NO_ORGANIZATION). Never add a member to a second organization.

  • Test company: a realm of the central Keycloak plays the company's identity provider: users with addresses in a test domain, and one confidential client whose redirect URI is the broker endpoint above.
  • EPITA: Identity providers, Microsoft, alias epita, Tenant ID 3534b3d7-316c-4bc9-9ede-605c860f49d2 (EPITA's tenant: only prenom.nom@epita.fr accounts get in). Client id and secret come from a Microsoft Entra app registration with the redirect URI of each realm (<p> and <p>-staging), multi-tenant if it is not registered in the EPITA tenant. Keycloak reads the profile from Microsoft Graph (User.Read, there by default). If the tenant blocks user consent, sign-in shows "admin approval required" and EPITA IT has to approve the app. Domain epita.fr. The CRI (https://cri.epita.fr, used by the Forge) has no dynamic registration: a client there must be requested.

Warning

manage-users lets an app edit any user of its realm, including the group membership of brokered developers. A leaked app client secret therefore lets its holder edit any account of that realm: keep app secrets tight.

Warning

The realm is shared by all apps of the project. With sign-up on, any self-registered account passes the SSO of every app exposed to "project users" (SSO without allowedGroups). Switch internal apps to "project members" before turning sign-up on.

docs.title: 6. Version and Upgrades
docs.text:
• Version: 26.8.1, set by image.tag in k8s/config/keycloak/values.yaml of the K3s repository.
  • Procedure: rehearse on a copy of the Keycloak database, take a pg_dump just before, then upgrade. The schema migrations of 26.6 and 26.8 are one-way: the rollback is the previous image plus the restored dump, not a downgrade in place.
  • Sessions: since 26.7, session cookies use SHA-384, so every user logs in once again after the upgrade.
  • Open point: the Keycloak database has no scheduled backup (follow-up). Until then, the pg_dump taken before an upgrade is the only copy.

Next Step: Continue to ArgoCD GitOps Delivery Specifications (or return to the Project Overview).

docs.title: Secrets Management: HashiCorp Vault
docs.text: CNP utilizes HashiCorp Vault for centralized, secure, and dynamic secret injection. No secrets are ever stored in plain text in GitHub, ArgoCD, or the CMP database.

docs.title: 1. Secrets Architecture Overview
docs.text:
The secrets pipeline is split into two access vectors: Human-to-Machine (OIDC) for developer administration, and Machine-to-Machine (Kubernetes Auth) for automated application syncing.

flowchart TD
    %% --- Access Vectors ---
    subgraph Human Access [Human-to-Machine]
        Dev[👤 Developer] -->|1. Login with SSO| V_UI[Vault Web UI]
        V_UI -->|2. Federates Auth| KC[Keycloak IdP]
        KC -->|3. Maps OIDC Groups to Policies| V_UI
    end

    subgraph Machine Access [Machine-to-Machine]
        K3s_Pod[Application Pod] <-->|6. Mounts Secret| K8s_Sec[K8s Secret]
        VSO[Vault Secrets Operator] -->|5. Reconciles & Decrypts| K8s_Sec
        VSO <-->|4. Authenticates via ServiceAccount| Vault_Engine[Vault KV V2 Engine]
    end

    %% Vault Core
    Vault_Engine -->|Enforces project-alpha-policy| Path_Alpha[kvv2/projects/alpha/*]

docs.title: 2. Developer Experience (Human OIDC Access)
docs.text: Developers access the Vault UI using their unified Keycloak credentials. Vault delegates authentication to Keycloak via the oidc auth path.

docs.title: A. Keycloak OIDC Mapping
docs.text: Vault is configured with an OIDC authentication backend. The Keycloak groups claim in the JWT is used to dynamically map the developer's project groups (project-<name>-members or project-<name>-admins) to specific Vault policies.

docs.title: B. Project Policy Template
docs.text:
During Day-0 project bootstrapping, Terraform writes a scoped policy restricting the developer's access to their project's path:

# project-alpha-dev-policy
path "sys/mounts" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}
path "sys/internal/ui/mounts/*" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}

# Grants full CRUD capabilities inside the project sandbox
path "project-alpha/*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "delete", "list"]
}

docs.title: 3. Application Experience (Machine Access via VSO)
docs.text: Pods retrieve secrets using the Vault Secrets Operator (VSO) (ricoberger.de/v1alpha1), ensuring that no raw Vault tokens are ever injected into application manifests.

docs.title: A. The Kubernetes Auth Flow
docs.text:
1. The application Pod starts in the alpha-frontend namespace.
  2. The VSO (acting on behalf of the namespace) presents its local Kubernetes ServiceAccount JWT token to Vault's /v1/auth/kubernetes/login endpoint.
  3. Vault validates the token against the K3s API server and checks that the ServiceAccount belongs to the allowed namespace (alpha-frontend).
  4. Vault returns a short-lived token bound to the application's policy.
  5. VSO decrypts the path, generates a native Kubernetes Secret, and mounts it to the Pod.

docs.title: B. Terraform Auth Role Provisioning
docs.text:
This secure handshake is made possible by the scoped Kubernetes auth role provisioned during Day-0:

# Terraform-generated Vault Auth Role
resource "vault_kubernetes_auth_backend_role" "app_role" {
  backend                          = "kubernetes"
  role_name                        = "alpha-frontend-role"
  bound_service_account_names      = ["vault-secrets-operator"]
  bound_service_account_namespaces = ["alpha-frontend"] # Hard boundary
  token_ttl                        = 3600
  token_policies                   = ["project-alpha-policy"]
}

docs.title: C. The Application Manifest (VaultSecret CRD)
docs.text:
ArgoCD deploys the following resource alongside the application deployment to trigger the synchronization:

apiVersion: ricoberger.de/v1alpha1
kind: VaultSecret
metadata:
  name: frontend-secrets
  namespace: alpha-frontend
  annotations:
    # Forces ArgoCD to sync the secret before creating deployment pods
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-1"
spec:
  # Path inside the isolated project KV engine
  path: kvv2/data/projects/alpha/frontend
  vaultRole: alpha-frontend-role
  type: Opaque

Next Step: Continue to ArgoCD GitOps Delivery Specifications (or return to the Project Overview).

docs.title: GitOps Delivery: ArgoCD Configuration
docs.text:
ArgoCD is the core Continuous Delivery (CD) engine of the CNP platform, responsible for reconciling the desired state declared in Git with the live state of the K3s cluster.

Given CNP's multi-tenant architecture, ArgoCD is configured to enforce strict tenancy barriers using native AppProject specifications, OIDC identity sync, and advanced mutation diffing strategies.

docs.title: 1. Single Sign-On (SSO) & Keycloak RBAC Mappings
docs.text: ArgoCD delegates authentication to Keycloak. Developers use a single login session across both the CMP and the ArgoCD control panels.

docs.title: OIDC Configuration (argocd-cm)
docs.text:
ArgoCD is patched to connect directly to the Keycloak 3istor realm, requesting the custom groups scope to extract the user's project affiliations.

# k8s/config/argocd/patch-argocd-cm.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: argocd-cm
  namespace: argocd
data:
  admin.enabled: "false" # Disables local fallback admin account
  url: "https://argocd.3istor.com"
  oidc.config: |
    name: 3Istor ID
    issuer: https://auth.3istor.com/realms/3istor
    clientID: argocd
    clientSecret: $oidc.keycloak.clientSecret # Synced from Vault
    requestedScopes: ["openid", "profile", "email", "groups"]

docs.title: Global RBAC Policies (argocd-rbac-cm)
docs.text:
To prevent unauthorized cluster access, all actions are blocked by default. Global permissions are assigned based on Keycloak groups:

# k8s/config/argocd/patch-argocd-rbac-cm.yaml
data:
  policy.default: "role:denied"
  scopes: "[groups]"
  policy.csv: |
    # Global cluster admins
    g, infra, role:admin

    # Global read-only access
    g, member, role:readonly

docs.title: 2. Multi-Tenancy Boundaries (AppProject)
docs.text:
CNP isolates teams using ArgoCD's AppProject resource. During Day-0 project bootstrapping, the CMP's project-base Helm chart deploys a dedicated AppProject matching the tenant.

# cnp-project-base/templates/app-project.yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AppProject
metadata:
  name: {{ .Values.projectName }}
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  description: "Isolated boundaries for project {{ .Values.projectName }}"
  sourceRepos: ["*"]

  # Crucial: Restricts this project to namespaces starting with the project prefix
  destinations:
    - namespace: "{{ .Values.projectName }}-*"
      server: "https://kubernetes.default.svc"

  # Whitelist standard resources
  namespaceResourceWhitelist:
    - group: "*"
      kind: "*"

  # Project-specific roles bound to OIDC groups
  roles:
    - name: "project-admins"
      description: "Admin privileges for {{ .Values.projectName }}"
      policies:
        - "p, proj:{{ .Values.projectName }}:project-admins, applications, *, {{ .Values.projectName }}/*, allow"
      groups: ["project-{{ .Values.projectName }}-admins"]

    - name: "project-members"
      description: "Read-only privileges for {{ .Values.projectName }}"
      policies:
        - "p, proj:{{ .Values.projectName }}:project-members, applications, get, {{ .Values.projectName }}/*, allow"
      groups: ["project-{{ .Values.projectName }}-members"]

docs.title: Security Isolation Rules:
docs.text:
• Destination Restriction: Apps within the alpha project can only be deployed to namespaces starting with alpha- (e.g., alpha-frontend, alpha-backend).
  • RBAC Scoping: Keycloak group members (project-alpha-admins) are mapped only to policies scoped to proj:alpha:project-admins, preventing cross-tenant visibility.

docs.title: 3. Resolving Kyverno Mutating Webhook Loops
docs.text: The cluster enforces security and resource policies using Kyverno. However, Kyverno's mutating webhooks (which inject default values like security contexts or resource limits if they are missing from Git) can cause infinite reconciliation loops with ArgoCD.

docs.title: The Conflict Loop:
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Git as GitHub (Desired State)
    participant Argo as ArgoCD Controller
    participant API as K8s API Server
    participant Kyverno as Kyverno Mutating Webhook

    Argo->>Git: Reads manifest (No securityContext defined)
    Argo->>API: 1. Compares with dry-run apply (Client-side Diff)
    API->>Kyverno: Intercepts request
    Kyverno->>API: Injects: securityContext.runAsNonRoot = true
    API-->>Argo: Returns mutated manifest
    Note over Argo: Detected Drift!<br/>Git has no securityContext,<br/>but dry-run has it.
    Argo->>API: 2. Reverts the mutation (Tries to delete runAsNonRoot)
    API->>Kyverno: Intercepts again
    Kyverno->>API: Reinjects: runAsNonRoot = true
    Note over Argo, API: Infinite OutOfSync loop!

docs.title: The Resolution (Server-Side Apply & ServerSideDiff)
docs.text:
To break this loop, CNP configures the application runner to calculate diffs and merges Server-Side instead of client-side.

By utilizing Server-Side Apply, the Kubernetes API server itself handles the merge resolution and ownership of fields. By utilizing ServerSideDiff, ArgoCD queries the API server after all mutating webhooks have executed, eliminating fake drift detections.

# Injected into the Application CRD by CMP Terraform
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: project-alpha-frontend
  namespace: argocd
  annotations:
    # 1. Calculates diff against post-mutation state
    argocd.argoproj.io/compare-options: ServerSideDiff=true,IncludeMutationWebhook=true
spec:
  project: project-alpha
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/my-org/project-alpha-frontend.git
    targetRevision: HEAD
    path: .
    helm:
      valueFiles:
        - deploy/values.yaml
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: project-alpha-frontend
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
    syncOptions:
      # 2. Delegates merge responsibility to K8s API server
      - ServerSideApply=true
      - CreateNamespace=true

Next Step: Continue to Terraform Provisioner & State Management Specs (or return to the Project Overview).

docs.title: GitHub Integration: Dedicated GitHub App Model
docs.text: To enforce the principle of least privilege, CNP completely rejects the use of global Personal Access Tokens (PATs). Instead, it implements a decentralized GitHub App integration model using a dedicated App (e.g., CNP-Portal, ID: 3836905) installed on user or organization accounts.

docs.title: 1. Onboarding & Linking Lifecycle
docs.text:
The onboarding process connects a developer's Keycloak identity to their GitHub organization installation, persisting the state inside both Keycloak user attributes and the CMP SQLite database.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Dev as Developer
    participant UI as CMP Frontend (Next.js)
    participant GH as GitHub App Portal
    participant API as CMP Backend (FastAPI)
    participant DB as SQLite (user_github_installations)
    participant KC as Keycloak Admin API

    Dev->>UI: Click "Link GitHub Account"
    UI->>GH: Redirects to https://github.com/apps/cnp-portal/installations/new
    Note over GH: User selects org/personal account<br/>and approves app permissions
    GH-->>UI: Redirect back with ?installation_id=98765432

    UI->>API: POST /account/github-installation {"installation_id": "98765432"}

    critical State Persistence
        API->>DB: Write/Update UserGitHubInstallation (user_sub, installation_id)
        API->>KC: Update custom user attribute "github_installation_id"
    end

    API-->>UI: Return 200 OK
    UI->>UI: Clean URL query parameters
    UI-->>Dev: UI displays "✅ GitHub linked"

docs.title: 2. GitHub App Permissions Matrix
docs.text:
The CNP-Portal GitHub App is configured with minimal, highly scoped permissions to perform automated repository management and GitOps write-backs:

Scope Permission Purpose Repository: Administration Read & Write Creating new repositories on Day-0 and configuring branch protection. Repository: Contents Read & Write Bootstrapping the code template and committing Day-2 config updates. Repository: Metadata Read-only Accessing repository basic structure (Required by GitHub). Repository: Webhooks Read & Write Subscribing to push events to notify CMP of developer updates.

docs.title: 3. Token Generation Workflow (Backend Mechanics)
docs.text: Whenever the SAGA orchestrator or the project bootstrapper needs to interact with GitHub, it generates a short-lived Installation Access Token (valid for 60 minutes) dynamically using the App's private key (GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY stored securely in Vault).

docs.title: A. Step 1: Generate signed JWT (Expires in 10 minutes)
docs.text:
The backend signs a JWT using the RS256 algorithm with the GitHub App private key: 

# app/services/github_service.py extract
def generate_jwt() -> str:
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    payload = {
        "iat": int(now.timestamp()),
        "exp": int((now + timedelta(minutes=10)).timestamp()),
        "iss": "3836905", # GitHub App ID
    }
    return jwt.encode(payload, settings.GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY, algorithm="RS256")

docs.title: B. Step 2: Request Installation Access Token
docs.text:
The JWT is exchanged for a scoped token: 

# app/services/github_service.py extract
async def get_installation_token(installation_id: str) -> str:
    app_jwt = generate_jwt()
    url = f"https://api.github.com/app/installations/{installation_id}/access_tokens"
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {app_jwt}",
        "Accept": "application/vnd.github+json",
        "X-GitHub-Api-Version": "2022-11-28",
    }
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        response = await client.post(url, headers=headers)
        return response.json()["token"]

docs.title: 4. ArgoCD Private Repository Access
docs.text:
To allow ArgoCD to sync the newly created private repository, Terraform configures ArgoCD with the GitHub App credentials directly using a dedicated K8s Secret. This allows ArgoCD to dynamically rotate its own tokens to pull the code.

# Configured via Terraform during Day-0 Bootstrapping
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: private-repo-creds
  namespace: argocd
  labels:
    argocd.argoproj.io/secret-type: repository
stringData:
  type: git
  url: "https://github.com/my-user-org/my-new-app.git"
  githubAppID: "3836905"
  githubAppInstallationID: "98765432"
  githubAppPrivateKey: | # Injected securely via TF_VAR_github_app_private_key

Next Step: Continue to App Provisioning Flow (or return to the Project Overview).

docs.title: Database Schema & Data Models
docs.text: The Cloud Native Platform (CNP) backend uses a relational database model (SQLite for development/light production, PostgreSQL for highly available enterprise setups) managed by SQLAlchemy 2.0 ORM. Schema migrations are tracked incrementally using Alembic.

docs.title: 1. Entity-Relationship Diagram (ERD)
docs.text:
The database schema isolates deployment states, immutable project creator ownerships, and user-to-GitHub App installations.

erDiagram
    deployments {
        int id PK "Autoincrement"
        string name "Unique"
        string template_id
        string status "Enum (pending, running, etc.)"
        string step_message
        string provider_type "Enum (legacy_hybrid, kubernetes)"
        string project_id "Index / Keycloak Group"
        string github_repo_url
        string argocd_app_name
        string k8s_namespace
        text terraform_outputs "JSON string"
        string terraform_state_path
        int resource_count
        text app_config "JSON string"
        string template_name
        string template_icon
        string template_category
        datetime created_at
        datetime updated_at
    }

    project_owners {
        int id PK "Autoincrement"
        string project_name "Unique, Index"
        string owner_username "Keycloak sub/username"
        datetime created_at
    }

    user_github_installations {
        int id PK "Autoincrement"
        string user_sub "Unique, Index"
        string installation_id
        datetime created_at
        datetime updated_at
    }

    project_owners ||--o{ deployments : "groups virtual machines & apps"

docs.title: A. deployments Table
docs.text:
This is a polymorphic table storing both legacy hybrid configurations (AWS + OpenStack IDs) and K3s GitOps configuration metadata.

Column Type Constraints Description id Integer Primary Key Autoincremented identifier. name String(100) Unique, Not Null Unique name generated for the application instance. template_id String(50) Not Null ID of the deployed template from the Catalog. status Enum Not Null Operational state (e.g., pending, running, failed). step_message String(255) Not Null Human-readable progress description or error dump. provider_type Enum Not Null, Default: LEGACY_HYBRID Discriminator: LEGACY_HYBRID or KUBERNETES. project_id String(100) Nullable References the Keycloak Project Group. github_repo_url String(255) Nullable Link to the created private GitOps repository. argocd_app_name String(100) Nullable Reconciled Application CRD name in ArgoCD. k8s_namespace String(100) Nullable Deployed namespace (<project_id>-<name>). terraform_outputs Text Nullable JSON string containing parsed Terraform output variables. terraform_state_path String(255) Nullable S3 bucket key pointing to the isolated .tfstate file. resource_count Integer Default: 0 Number of live resources managed by this micro-state. app_config Text Nullable Raw JSON parameters supplied by the developer.

docs.title: B. project_owners Table
docs.text:
Stores the immutable creator of a project. While standard project membership lives inside Keycloak groups, the creator is mapped here to guarantee permanent ownership rights.

Column Type Constraints Description id Integer Primary Key Autoincremented identifier. project_name String(100) Unique, Index, Not Null Unique identifier of the project (lowercase kebab-case). owner_username String(255) Not Null Keycloak username of the creator. created_at DateTime Default: now() Generation timestamp.

docs.title: C. user_github_installations Table
docs.text:
Maps the developer's unique Keycloak subject claim (sub) to their GitHub App installation identifier. This allows the backend to generate dynamic GitHub access tokens on behalf of the user.

Column Type Constraints Description id Integer Primary Key Autoincremented identifier. user_sub String(255) Unique, Index, Not Null Keycloak user UUID (sub claim). installation_id String(100) Not Null Installation token identifier returned by GitHub.

docs.title: 3. Data Ownership & Security Boundaries
docs.text:
CNP enforces split-ownership boundaries. Database tables are segmented between Global metadata and User/Tenant metadata:

                              ┌────────────────────────────────┐
                              │    User Security Context       │
                              │    (Keycloak JWT Groups)       │
                              └───────────────┬────────────────┘
                                              │
                     ┌────────────────────────┴────────────────────────┐
                     ▼                                                 ▼
        ┌─────────────────────────┐                       ┌─────────────────────────┐
        │  User/Tenant Owned      │                       │     Global Metadata     │
        ├─────────────────────────┤                       ├─────────────────────────┤
        │ • user_github_install   │                       │ • deployments table     │
        │ • project_owners        │                       │ • template configurations│
        └─────────────────────────┘                       └─────────────────────────┘
  • Tenant Boundary Filtering: Although the deployments table is technically global, the CMP backend filters queries at the API layer. A user can only see or mutate a deployment if their Keycloak JWT contains the project-<project_id>-admins or project-<project_id>-members group claim corresponding to the deployment's project_id.

docs.title: A. Application Deployment Lifecycle (K8s / GitOps)
docs.text:
The state machine transitions sequentially. If a step fails during Day-0, the state is forced into failed and SAGA compensations are executed.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> pending : POST /api/deployments
    pending --> initializing : Saga Orchestrator picks up task
    initializing --> planning : Git App Template cloned / customized
    planning --> deploying : terraform apply executes
    deploying --> running : Day-0 Success / Handover to ArgoCD
    deploying --> failed : Terraform / Git error (Trigger rollback)

    running --> degraded : Gatus polls 5xx or ArgoCD reports OutOfSync
    degraded --> running : Self-healing / Manual sync success

    running --> deleting : DELETE /api/deployments/{id}
    deleting --> deleted : terraform destroy success
    deleted --> [*] : Database record marked deleted

docs.title: A. SQLite Concurrency: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)
docs.text:
Because the CMP Backend executes heavy background tasks (like shell processes running Terraform), SQLite can easily experience database locks. To prevent queries from freezing, the platform explicitly configures SQLite connection pools to use WAL Mode:

# app/core/database.py
@event.listens_for(engine, "connect")
def set_sqlite_pragma(dbapi_connection, connection_record):
    cursor = dbapi_connection.cursor()
    cursor.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;")
    cursor.execute("PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL;")
    cursor.close()

docs.title: B. Alembic Migrations
docs.text:
Migrations are managed incrementally. For example, to migrate the schema from Phase 2 to Phase 3 (adding multi-provider columns), Alembic executes the following operations:

# alembic/versions/c4d8f2a91b3e_add_kubernetes_provider_support.py
def upgrade() -> None:
    op.add_column('deployments', sa.Column('provider_type', sa.Enum('LEGACY_HYBRID', 'KUBERNETES', name='providertype'), nullable=False, server_default='LEGACY_HYBRID'))
    op.add_column('deployments', sa.Column('project_id', sa.String(100), nullable=True))
    op.add_column('deployments', sa.Column('github_repo_url', sa.String(255), nullable=True))
    op.add_column('deployments', sa.Column('argocd_app_name', sa.String(100), nullable=True))
    op.add_column('deployments', sa.Column('k8s_namespace', sa.String(100), nullable=True))

Next Step: Continue to Frontend Architecture Specification (or return to the Project Overview).

docs.title: Architecture Frontend : Portail CMP (Next.js) ⚡
docs.text:
Ce document décrit l'architecture technique du Frontend de la Cloud Management Platform (CMP), développée en Next.js (React). Il détaille la structure des répertoires, l'arborescence des composants, le cycle de vie de la session utilisateur OIDC (Keycloak JWT) et les mécanismes de mise à jour de l'état en temps réel.

Pour des informations complémentaires, consultez : * L'architecture globale du portail : 01-cmp-dashboard.md * L'intégration avec Keycloak : 02-identity-keycloak.md * Le guide d'intégration API Phase 4 : 03-cmp-frontend-integration.md * Le contrat d'API de déploiement : 01-cmp-deployment-api.md

docs.title: 📂 Structure du Répertoire Frontend
docs.text:
L'application utilise le Next.js App Router avec l'arborescence src/app/ pour définir les routes et gérer le rendu (côté serveur et côté client).

frontend/src/
├── app/                         # Dossier racine du Next.js App Router
│   ├── layout.tsx               # Layout principal (Nav, Providers d'authentification)
│   ├── page.tsx                 # Page d'accueil / Tableau de bord global
│   ├── auth/
│   │   └── callback/            # Point de retour OIDC (Keycloak Login Callback)
│   ├── catalog/
│   │   └── page.tsx             # Catalogue de templates (Dual Tabs : PaaS vs IaaS)
│   ├── projects/
│   │   └── [id]/                # Détail d'un projet (Applications, configuration GitOps, Membres)
│   └── account/
│       └── page.tsx             # Gestion de compte, liaison GitHub
├── components/                  # Composants UI React réutilisables
│   ├── account/                 # GitHubLinkButton (Bouton OAuth)
│   ├── catalog/                 # CatalogGrid, DeployModal (Formulaires)
│   ├── dashboard/               # Widgets de statistiques et statuts globaux
│   ├── projects/                # AppCard, AppConfigPanel (Editeur yaml), MembersPanel
│   └── ui/                      # Composants génériques bas niveau (boutons, inputs, etc.)
├── lib/                         # Logique utilitaire et clients API
│   ├── api-client.ts            # Client HTTP configuré avec injecteur JWT
│   └── keycloak-context.tsx     # Contexte React d'authentification (session client)
└── types/                       # Interfaces TypeScript partagées (Deployment, Project)

docs.title: 🗺️ Arborescence des Composants UI
docs.text:
Le schéma suivant montre comment les layouts, providers et composants de pages s'agencent :

graph TD
    %% Layout et Providers
    Layout["RootLayout (app/layout.tsx)"] --> Providers["KeycloakProvider (keycloak-context.tsx)"]
    Providers --> Nav["SideBar / Navigation layout"]

    %% Pages Principales

docs.title: 🔑 Gestion de la Session Utilisateur (JWT Keycloak)
docs.text: L'authentification s'appuie sur le protocole OpenID Connect (OIDC) géré par Keycloak.

docs.title: 1. Cinématique d'Authentification (Authorization Code Flow)
docs.text:
1. Redirection vers l'IdP : Si l'utilisateur n'est pas connecté, le composant KeycloakProvider intercepte la route et redirige le navigateur vers Keycloak (/auth/realms/kube-lab/protocol/openid-connect/auth).
  2. Retour de code d'autorisation : Après authentification et validation MFA, Keycloak redirige l'utilisateur vers /auth/callback?code=CODE.
  3. Échange et récupération du JWT : La page de callback capture le code temporaire et appelle le endpoint /token de Keycloak pour obtenir trois jetons :
  4. access_token (JWT à courte durée de vie, par exemple 15 minutes).
  5. refresh_token (Jeton persistant pour renouveler l'accès).
  6. id_token (Informations sur l'identité de l'utilisateur).

docs.title: 2. Stockage et Sécurité du Jeton
docs.text: Pour limiter les risques de failles de sécurité XSS (Cross-Site Scripting), le client applique les règles suivantes : * L'access_token est conservé uniquement en mémoire dans le contexte React (KeycloakContext). Il n'est jamais écrit dans le localStorage ou le sessionStorage. * Le refresh_token est géré de manière sécurisée par l'intégration keycloak-js (via des cookies ou un stockage de session isolé) permettant le renouvellement transparent du jeton d'accès en arrière-plan sans perturber l'expérience utilisateur.

docs.title: 3. Interception et Injection API
docs.text:
Pour communiquer avec le Backend FastAPI du CMP, toutes les requêtes HTTP passent par un client d'API personnalisé (api-client.ts). Cet outil intercepte l'envoi et injecte dynamiquement l'en-tête d'authentification :

// Extrait conceptuel de lib/api-client.ts
async function fetchWithAuth(url: string, options: RequestInit = {}) {
  // Récupère le token valide depuis le contexte en mémoire
  const token = await getValidToken(); 

  const headers = {
    ...options.headers,
    'Authorization': `Bearer ${token}`,
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
  };

  return fetch(url, { ...options, headers });
}

docs.title: 📡 Rafraîchissement et Streaming de l'État Global
docs.text: Le suivi des statuts de déploiements (PENDING ➔ PROVISIONING ➔ RUNNING) et l'affichage des journaux d'exécution Terraform nécessitent des stratégies différentes pour minimiser la consommation réseau tout en garantissant une réactivité immédiate.

docs.title: 1. Streaming des Logs en Temps Réel (Server-Sent Events)
docs.text:
Lors du bootstrapping initial (Day-0) d'une application ou d'un rollback SAGA, le runner Terraform écrit continuellement des logs de sortie. Le Frontend CMP utilise les Server-Sent Events (SSE) (technologie W3C native) pour streamer ce flux de logs sans l'overhead des WebSockets.

  • Mécanique technique :
  • Le Frontend initie une connexion persistante via la classe JavaScript EventSource.
  • Le backend FastAPI envoie des trames de données de type text/event-stream.

  • L'application met à jour le composant LogsStreamPanel au fil de l'eau.

  • Exemple d'implémentation client : 

    // components/projects/LogsStreamPanel.tsx
import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

export function LogsStreamPanel({ deploymentId }: { deploymentId: number }) {
  const [logs, setLogs] = useState<string[]>([]);

  useEffect(() => {
    // Les requêtes SSE standards du navigateur ne supportent pas nativement
    // l'envoi d'en-têtes personnalisés (Authorization: Bearer).
    // CNP passe donc le token de session via un paramètre de requête HTTP :
    const token = getCachedToken();
    const eventSource = new EventSource(`/api/deployments/${deploymentId}/logs/stream?token=${token}`);

    eventSource.onmessage = (event) => {
      // Ajout de la ligne de log reçue dans le terminal virtuel
      setLogs((prevLogs) => [...prevLogs, event.data]);
    };

    eventSource.onerror = (error) => {
      console.error("Erreur de flux SSE :", error);
      eventSource.close();
    };

    return () => {
      eventSource.close(); // Ferme la socket lorsque le composant est démonté
    };
  }, [deploymentId]);

  return (
    <pre className="bg-black text-green-400 p-4 rounded overflow-y-auto max-h-96">
      {logs.map((log, idx) => <div key={idx}>{log}</div>)}
    </pre>
  );
}

docs.title: 2. Rafraîchissement des Métadonnées & Statuts (Polling)
docs.text:
Pour les informations moins denses mais nécessitant une cohérence temporelle (comme le statut général d'un déploiement ou l'état de synchronisation d'ArgoCD), le Frontend utilise le concept de Short Polling contrôlé par React Query / SWR.

  • Fonctionnement :
  • Si l'application affiche un statut transitionnel (PENDING ou PROVISIONING), React Query configure une fréquence de rafraîchissement élevée (refetchInterval: 5000 soit toutes les 5 secondes).
  • Dès que le statut passe à un état stable (RUNNING, DEGRADED, ou FAILED), le rafraîchissement automatique est désactivé (refetchInterval: false) pour économiser les ressources de la base de données et du serveur.
// lib/hooks/useDeployment.ts
import { useQuery } from "@tanstack/react-query";

export function useDeployment(id: number) {
  return useQuery({
    queryKey: ["deployment", id],
    queryFn: () => fetchWithAuth(`/api/deployments/${id}`).then(res => res.json()),
    // Désactive le polling si le déploiement n'est plus en cours de modification
    refetchInterval: (query) => {
      const status = query.state.data?.status;
      return (status === "PENDING" || status === "PROVISIONING") ? 5000 : false;
    }
  });
}
